title: 2 Kings 18:1–12
context: Hezekiah son of Ahaz begins to reign in Judah, and unlike his father (2 Kings 16:2–3) he does what is right in the LORD’s eyes, removing the high places and even breaking the bronze serpent Moses had made, because Israel had burned incense to it. The narrator praises his trust in the LORD as unmatched among the kings of Judah, notes his rebellion against Assyria, and then recalls the fall of Samaria to Assyria because Israel did not obey the LORD’s voice (compare 2 Kings 17:7). The synchronisms between Hezekiah’s reign, Hoshea’s reign, and the later invasion in 18:13 are difficult to fit together, and interpreters reconstruct the dates in different ways, so exact years are best held with caution. Arminian and Reformed readers commonly treat the passage as shared ground about wholehearted reform, trust in the LORD, and the sober contrast between Judah’s faithful king and Israel’s exile.

verses.text: Now in the third year of Hoshea son of Elah king of Israel, Hezekiah the son of Ahaz king of Judah began to reign.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Hezekiah beginning his reign while Israel’s last king still rules in Samaria. A new king brings a new opportunity for Judah to return wholeheartedly to the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God raising up a faithful king at a critical moment in Judah’s history. Readers in both traditions commonly hold the exact chronology of the reign with caution.

verses.text: He was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Abi the daughter of Zechariah.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note Hezekiah’s age, the length of his reign, and his mother’s name, Abi the daughter of Zechariah. The regnal formula places his reign within Judah’s ongoing story.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the formula as framing a reign that the narrator will evaluate by faithfulness to the LORD. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a standard introduction.

verses.text: He did that which was right in the LORD’s eyes, according to all that David his father had done.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Hezekiah doing right in the LORD’s eyes, like David his father. His choices break sharply with the pattern of his father Ahaz (2 Kings 16:2–3).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the comparison with David as the highest praise the narrator gives a king. Readers in both traditions commonly see God’s grace at work in a reformer who arose from an unfaithful home.

verses.text: He removed the high places, broke the pillars, and cut down the Asherah. He also broke in pieces the bronze serpent that Moses had made, because in those days the children of Israel burned incense to it; and he called it Nehushtan.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Hezekiah removing the high places and breaking the bronze serpent, which had become an object of incense. Even something God once used can become an idol when trust shifts to it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the destruction of Nehushtan as zeal for pure worship, though the serpent had served God’s purpose (Numbers 21:9; compare John 3:14). Both traditions commonly read the verse as a warning against honoring the gift above the Giver.

verses.text: He trusted in the LORD, the God of Israel, so that after him was no one like him among all the kings of Judah, nor among them that were before him.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Hezekiah’s trust in the LORD as the defining mark of his reign. Faith is the heart of the narrator’s praise, not military or political success.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see his unmatched trust as God’s gift displayed in a king. Readers in both traditions commonly note that 2 Kings 23:25 gives similar praise to Josiah for wholehearted turning, so each king is praised for a particular excellence.

verses.text: For he joined with the LORD. He didn’t depart from following him, but kept his commandments, which the LORD commanded Moses.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Hezekiah holding fast to the LORD and keeping his commandments. Faithfulness is shown in continued obedience, not only in a single reform.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see his perseverance in following the LORD as the fruit of genuine faith. Both traditions commonly read the verse as describing a life shaped by the law given through Moses.

verses.text: The LORD was with him. Wherever he went, he prospered. He rebelled against the king of Assyria, and didn’t serve him.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD with Hezekiah, prospering him and enabling his rebellion against Assyria. Faithfulness and blessing are closely linked in the narrative.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s presence as the source of Hezekiah’s success. Readers in both traditions commonly avoid turning the verse into a promise that faith always brings worldly prosperity.

verses.text: He struck the Philistines to Gaza and its borders, from the tower of the watchmen to the fortified city.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Hezekiah striking the Philistines as far as Gaza. His reign includes military strength alongside religious reform.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see these victories as further signs of the LORD being with him. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a brief summary of his early success.

verses.text: In the fourth year of King Hezekiah, which was the seventh year of Hoshea son of Elah king of Israel, Shalmaneser king of Assyria came up against Samaria and besieged it.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Shalmaneser besieging Samaria in Hezekiah’s fourth year. Judah’s faithful king watches the northern kingdom fall.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the siege as the fulfillment of long warnings to Israel. Readers in both traditions commonly hold the precise dating of these events with caution.

verses.text: At the end of three years they took it. In the sixth year of Hezekiah, which was the ninth year of Hoshea king of Israel, Samaria was taken.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Samaria taken after three years. The end of the northern kingdom comes after a long siege and is complete.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s patience finally giving way to judgment. Both traditions commonly read the verse soberly as a sign of covenant consequences.

verses.text: The king of Assyria carried Israel away to Assyria, and put them in Halah, and on the Habor, the river of Gozan, and in the cities of the Medes,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Israel carried into exile and settled in distant places, including the cities of the Medes. The people lose the land that was given to them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see exile as the covenant curse long threatened for unfaithfulness. Readers in both traditions commonly hold the exact locations named here with caution.

verses.text: because they didn’t obey the LORD their God’s voice, but transgressed his covenant, even all that Moses the servant of the LORD commanded, and would not hear it or do it.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the reason given for exile: Israel did not obey the LORD’s voice and transgressed his covenant. The people bore real responsibility for their choices.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as a clear statement of covenant justice (compare 2 Kings 17:7). Both traditions commonly read it as a solemn warning set beside Hezekiah’s faithfulness.
